Consider lime to raise the pH toward the optimal range.

results.answer:
The north side is in the low‑productivity zone.  
This zone covers 33.4 % of the field and holds 92.3 acres.  
Etowah silt loam on 2‑to‑6 % slopes makes up 16.7 % of the low zone but only 10.3 % of the whole field.  
This soil has a pH of 5.0, below the optimal 6.0‑6.5 range.  
Etowah silt loam on 0‑to‑2 % slopes and Guthrie silt loam that floods occasionally are also in the low zone.  
Lobelville silt loam that floods occasionally and Wolftever silt loam are also concentrated in the low zone.  
These soils are less common in the rest of the field.  
Low pH and occasional flooding reduce root growth and nutrient uptake.  
Therefore the north side shows weaker cotton growth because it contains more low‑pH, flood‑prone soils that limit plant health.

results.answer:
Less summer rain reduces water excess on the crop.  
When rain is lower, the soil stays drier during boll set and fill.  
Drier conditions lower the risk of boll rot.  
The model shows summer rainfall this season 12.4 in. versus typical 14.6 in.  
The difference adds an 8.4 lb/acre positive effect to the yield estimate.  
Therefore the estimate rises when summer rain is below normal.

The season had a large drought deficit. Total rain was 27.9 inches. Water balance was –7.0 inches, showing a net loss. The longest dry spell lasted 24 days. Heat stress occurred on 20 days. Drought was strongest in July, when rain was only 2.6 inches and balance –3.8 inches. This level of deficit reduced soil moisture for cotton growth.
